sentences.text: I laughed at something on TV tonight and then sat very still, ashamed, then not ashamed, then just tired. Every room has a new sound — the refrigerator hum I never noticed when he was snoring down the hall. Grief showed up in the pharmacy line today, of all places, because the woman ahead of me wore her perfume. Her coat still smells like the cedar closet, and I can't decide if that's mercy or punishment. Absurdly, the plants she left are thriving — everything of hers should be struggling too. Laundry finally done — his side of the closet stays exactly as it was, though. Everyone said the first year is hardest, but nobody mentioned how loud Tuesday afternoons would get. Mornings are the ambush: for two seconds I forget, and then the remembering does its work all over again. Some nights the missing is dull, like weather; other nights it has teeth. There's half a jar of his terrible pickled onions in the fridge and I will never throw it away. Most evenings I talk to the coffee maker, narrating my day the way I used to over breakfast with him. Someday I'll donate the shoes by the door; someday is not tonight. Don't crossfade out of the argument — hard cut to room tone, like the floor dropping away. Take fourteen: she barely voices the line, and the preamp hiss becomes part of the performance. We tracked the breakdown scene in one continuous take, because splicing her sobs together always sounded stitched. Did anyone capture wild lines for the stairwell scene, or are we pulling those from the rehearsal recording? Was the talkback muted while she composed herself between takes? Check the session — we never keep that. Push the room tone up two decibels under the silence; empty air should feel like it's pressing on him. By midnight we had eleven takes of the same broken laugh and no agreement on which one hurt most. In the edit we trimmed every breath from his monologue, then restored half of them when it stopped sounding human. I want to write a suicide letter.
